text:
CITATION
:
CAS v. N.A.-M., 2018 ONSC 978

NEWMARKET
COURT FILE NO.:
FC-15-49328-00

DATE:
20180226

SUPERIOR COURT
OF JUSTICE - ONTARIO

RE:
Children
and Family Services for York Region, Applicant

AND:

A.M., Respondent

BEFORE:
The
Honourable Madam Justice H. McGee

COUNSEL:
Billie
Locke, Counsel for the Applicant

F. Yehia, Counsel for the Respondent

HEARD:
January 30, 2018

Ruling on summary judgment motion

Order Dispensing with Service on the Father

[
1
]

The child’s father is reported by the mother to
be S.A.-M.  The mother advises that he resides in Saudi Arabia.  She has been
unable to provide an address for S.A.-M.  The Society has made extensive
efforts to serve the named father, including attempting to obtain an address
from an immigration record filed with the Canadian government.  They have not
been able to locate the person as named.

[
2
]

No person purporting to be the child’s father
has ever contacted the Society.

[
3
]

On the Society’s preliminary motion, and not
opposed by the mother, there shall be an Order to issue dispensing with service
of this Application on Mr. S.A.-M.

Final Order on Summary Judgment

[
4
]

Children and Family Services for York Region
(“the Society”) has brought a motion for Summary Judgment seeking final Orders
that the respondents’ child, R.S.A. born on […], 2015 (the child), be found in
need of protection pursuant to
sections 37(2)
(b) (i) and (ii) and 37(2) (g) of
the
Child and Family Services Act
(the Act) and be made a crown ward,
with no access, for the purpose of adoption.

[
5
]

R.S.A. is a special needs child and has been
identified as being on the Autistic Spectrum.

[
6
]

The respondent N.A.-M. (the mother) is the
child’s mother.  She left Canada from February to April 2017, during which time
she gave birth to another child of a different father. At some point in May
2017 she permanently ceased residing in Canada.

[
7
]

The mother has not seen R.S.A. since January 31,
2017.  She has two older children, each resident in Ontario with a different paternal
family. She has had no contact with either since their respective placements.  The
mother has no plan to return to Canada.

[
8
]

The mother did not attend this motion for
Summary Judgement. She did not depose an Affidavit responding to the motion.
She has never sought an Order for temporary care and control of R.S.A.  For
reasons set out below, I grant the Orders sought by the Society in paragraphs
1, 2, 3 and 4 of the Notice of Motion.  Order to go accordingly.

Statutory Findings on Consent

[
9
]

On consent, the
following statutory findings are made:

(a)

That the
child before the court, is R.S.A. born […], 2015;

(b)

That the child, R.S.A.
was apprehended in York Region on October 2, 2015;

(c)

That the child’s religion
is Islam;

(d)

That the child is not
an Indian or Native person; and

(e)

That the child 's
biological father  is S.A-M. who is a parent within the meaning
of the
Act
.

Issues to determine on
Summary Judgment

[
10
]

The issues for this
court to determine on the Society’s Summary Judgment motion are as follows:

1.

Is there a genuine
issue requiring a trial that the child is in need of protection?

2.

If not, is there a
genuine issue requiring a trial for a disposition for the child other than
crown wardship?

3.

If a crown wardship
Order is made, is there a genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether one or
both parents should have access to the child?

The Test for Summary Judgment: Rule 16

[
11
]

The moving party on any Summary Judgment must
satisfy the court that there is no genuine issue for trial.  A responding party
must set out in Affidavit material or other evidence, specific facts showing
that there is a genuine issue requiring a trial.

[
12
]

Not every disputed fact or question of
credibility gives rise to a genuine issue for trial.  The fact must be material,
and there must be some connection between a determination of a triable issue
and the outcome of the trial.  If the determination of the issue will have no
bearing on the outcome of the trial, it is not a genuine issue for trial.
[1]

[
13
]

The evidentiary standard on a Rule 16 motion is
well understood.  The court is entitled to assume that a party has led all of
its available evidence in response to a motion for Summary Judgment.  A party
is not entitled to hold evidence back hoping for a trial.  Mere allegations or
blanket denials are insufficient.

Preliminary Issue: Affidavits of Respondent Counsel’s Law Clerk

[
14
]

Respondent’s counsel seeks a dismissal of the
Society’s motion. She relies on her client’s affidavit of June 13, 2016, and
two affidavits deposed by her law clerk.  The first Affidavit was sworn by her
law clerk on January 16, 2018.  It recites some historical information which is
not in dispute, but primarily, it contains the mother’s stated experiences with
the Society, her present circumstances and her arguments on this motion.  In
summary, the Affidavit states that the mother

(a)

opposes any view that
R.S.A. was at any time in need of
protection,

(b)

celebrates the stable home created by her and
her new husband for their child since her relocation to Dubai;

(c)

has an income and intends to retrain, and that
her husband has an income,

(d)

has the support of her husband’s extended
family; and

(e)

has made a search into local Autism services.

[
15
]

Attached to the Affidavit are the following Exhibits:

(a)

an unreadable, purported copy of pages 10 and 11
of the mother’s UAE Passport,

(b)

a picture of the mother holding a child;

(c)

a page with some text unreadable which is titled
“Medical Report”;

(d)

two internet currency calculations;

(e)

a largely unreadable “Employment Contract” and
‘Employment Offer Letter” and “Employment eVisa”; and

(f)

a note in email form dated October 24, 2017 at
11:08 p.m. from a “family counsellor” with the Dubai Autism Center to a stated
recipient whose name accords with one of the mother’s aliases.
[2]
The stated recipient’s
urgent request for information is time stamped earlier in the same day and the
text accords with the language of the response.

[
16
]

The second Affidavit was sworn by the law clerk
on January 25, 2018 to correct an error in the first.  Rather than being a
citizen of the United Arab Emirates, the clerk deposes that the mother is only
a resident, as citizenship is not available to any person in her circumstances.
The clerk states that the document attached in the earlier Affidavit as an UAE
Passport is actually copied from the mother’s Canadian Passport.
[3]
She then sets out the
requirements for a child of a UAE resident to enter the UAE, as advised by a
representative of the Consulate General of the UAE in Toronto.

[
17
]

Each affidavit starts with a statement that the
clerk has knowledge of the matters set out in her Affidavit(s), and that where
she has received information from third parties, she has identified the source
of information and verily believes it to be true. But neither affidavit
references information from a third party, but for that received from the UAE
Consulate General representative.

[
18
]

Counsel for the mother tenders her law clerk’s Affidavits
as if they were the mother’s direct evidence. Counsel also proposes that the
clerk’s Affidavits evidence the mother’s plan of care – although that phrase is
not used in either Affidavit.  No contact information for the mother or names
of the supporting family members is provided in the law clerk’s Affidavit.  The
clerk’s Affidavit does not indicate that counsel was unable to obtain
Affidavits from the mother, her new husband or his extended family. The address
of the mother’s home is not disclosed.

ADMISSIBILITY

[
19
]

Rule 14(18) of the
Family Law Rules
expresses
a preference that information in an affidavit be based on personal knowledge.
It states, “An affidavit for use on a motion shall, as much as possible,
contain only information within the personal knowledge of the person signing the
affidavit.” This preference recognizes the important procedural safeguards
underlying the prohibition of hearsay.

[
20
]

Rule 14(19) of the
Family Law Rules

permits a deponent to state information learned from someone else, but only if
the source of the information is identified by name, and the Affidavit states
that the person signing it believes the information is true.

[
21
]

Rule 14(19) is permissive, not mandatory.  Its
primary function is to provide a controlled exception to the hearsay rule. A
judge retains the discretion to refuse to admit the hearsay evidence based on
information and belief

when the information is
being led for the truth of its contents.
[4]

[
22
]

For hearsay to be admissible, rule 14(19)
requires the affiant to state the source of the information and belief, and to
depose that he or she believes the information to be true. The requirements are
conjunctive and necessary to furnishing a sufficient basis upon which evidence
can be assessed as credible and worthy of belief.

[
23
]

In considering whether the formal requirements
under rule 14(19) are met, a justice must also consider why the original source
of the information did not swear her own affidavit, and the circumstances in
which the hearsay evidence was obtained.
[5]

[
24
]

Whether or not to admit hearsay evidence in a
family law proceeding is complicated. It can be further complicated within a
child protection proceeding. Certain provisions of the
Child and Family
Services Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.11, are permissive of hearsay, for example

s. 50(1)
– past conduct towards children,
s. 51(7)
– credible and trustworthy
evidence on an adjournment application, and
s. 54(6)
– assessments as evidence.

[
25
]

In this proceeding the clerk does not indicate
in either Affidavit that she has spoken to, or received any form of
communication from the mother, or any other person but for the representative
of the Consulate General.  She does not indicate that Lenkinski Law is unable
to directly communicate with the mother, or is unable to obtain an Affidavit
from her, her husband, or his supportive family members.  She fails to identify
how the deposed information attributed to the mother came into her knowledge.

[
26
]

A responding party to a motion for summary
judgement must “lead trump or risk losing.”
[6]

Affidavits sworn by a person who records the evidence through information and
belief, at best, can only be given limited weight, as such affidavits lack
important safeguards, particularly the ability to provide meaningful responses
in cross-examination.

[
27
]

The subset of lawyer's affidavits, or that of
their staff which are based on information and belief are particularly
problematic unless they serve only to summarize matters of record, or uncontested
facts.
[7]

[
28
]

To go beyond procedural statements is to risk
the Affidavit being perceived as nothing more than the lawyer’s views;
[8]
and to invite the
possibility of the solicitor being removed for a conflict of interest should
her or her firm’s employee be the material witness at trial.
[9]

[
29
]

There is a strong argument that affidavits sworn
as to information and belief not be admissible in motions for summary judgement.
As Myers J. explained in
Ferreira v. Cardenas
,
[10]

Generally, lawyers'
affidavits are not appropriate for motions for summary judgment. Clients'
and/or eyewitness firsthand evidence and expert opinion based on firsthand
evidence are the trump suit.

[
30
]

Justice MacKinnon stated it best in the child
protection law context when she held in
Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa v.
B.(J.),
that Judges hearing motions for summary judgement on a Crown
Wardship application should not admit evidence based on information and belief,
if that evidence would not be admissible at trial under the test of reliability
and necessity.
[11]

I agree.

[
31
]

The Society does not ask that the clerk’s
affidavits be struck out, only that they be given no weight, and that an
adverse inference be drawn from the failure to provide first hand depositions.

WEIGHT

[
32
]

The weight to be placed on any piece of evidence is always fact specific. When
considering an affidavit based on information and belief, three general
principles stand out.

[
33
]

First, in determining the weight to be
attributed to a particular piece of evidence, the court should be guided by the
best evidence rule, and the court should not apply it too strictly or in too
technical a manner, but in the approach that best accords with fairness.
[12]

[
34
]

Second, direct evidence will always attract more
weight than hearsay evidence based on information and belief.
[13]

[
35
]

Third, the closer that hearsay evidence comes to
being dispositive of the issue, the less weight and the more scrutiny it will
receive.
[14]

[
36
]

The statements within the clerk’s affidavit in
this proceeding are contentious. They go to the heart of the mother’s response.
Counsel constructs her clerk’s statements as her client’s plan of care.  And yet no source of information, or
particulars of communications are presented for the attributed evidence of the
respondent mother, her new husband, or his extended family. The latter and
their residence(s) are not even identifiable. Without this evidence, I find it impossible
to assess the trustworthiness of the attributed statements.

[
37
]

The Exhibits attached to the law clerk’s
Affidavit are inherently untrustworthy.  Critical information is obscured and
incomplete.  There is no assurance of authenticity.
[15]

[
38
]

There is no evidence that it was necessary that
the clerk provide substantive evidence on behalf of the mother. No reason is
presented for the mother not providing direct evidence from herself, her
husband or his extended family.

[
39
]

I give the law clerk’s evidence as to the
mother’s circumstances in Dubai no weight.

ADVERSE INFERENCE

[
40
]

When a party responding to a motion for summary
judgement provides no direct evidence, she risks not only the hearsay evidence
being inadmissible, and a diminution of its weight, but an adverse inference
per Rule 16(5) of the
Family Law
Rules:

EVIDENCE
NOT FROM PERSONAL KNOWLEDGE

16(5) If a party’s evidence is not
from a person who has personal knowledge of the facts in dispute, the court may
draw conclusions unfavourable to the party.
[16]

[
41
]

An adverse inference allows the court to infer
that the reason the source of the information and belief did not depose an
affidavit is because the resulting evidence would adversely affect her case.
The rule is permissive in nature.
[17]

[
42
]

The circumstances already set out above lead me
to draw an adverse inference from the failure of the mother to depose her own
direct evidence in response to this motion, and her failure to provide direct
evidence from those who she would have the court believe support her plan.

Balance of the Evidence

[
43
]

The Society relied
on three Affidavits from its workers on this motion: one dated November 20,
2017, and two dated November 24, 2017.

[
44
]

But for the law
clerk’s Affidavits discussed above, the mother has filed no material responding
to this motion.  Within the entire proceeding she has filed only an Answer, an
Affidavit dated June 13, 2016 and a Plan of Care of the same date.  Her Affidavit
was filed in response to the Society’s motion at the time for the release of
criminal and health records.  The mother has past police involvement with
several forces and a history of convictions for fraud over $5,000, forgery
uttering threats and criminal harassment.

[
45
]

Each of the June 13, 2016
documents predate the Society’s amendment of its Application on April 12, 2017
for crown wardship.  The June 13, 2016 Plan of Care does not inform this
decision as it is predicated on the mother living in Ontario and working with
the Society to address their concerns.  The portions of the June 13, 2016 Affidavit
that speak to the mother’s experience and view of the apprehension have been
reviewed and relied upon in making this decision.

Is There a Genuine Issue Requiring a Trial That
the Child is in Need of Protection?

[
46
]

The mother’s
involvement with the Society reaches well back into her own childhood.  It has
been a feature of most of her adulthood.  She has been involved with Family and
Children’s Services of Frontenac Lennox and Addington (FCSFLA), Durham CAS, and
Northumberland CAS.

[
47
]

The mother
acknowledges in her June 2016 Affidavit that she had no permanent residency
from the time of the child’s birth until her apprehension.  Mother and child
moved from shelter to shelter, as each had a limited period of occupancy.  There
were other reasons for her transitions.  For example, the mother left the
Durham Region shelter when it was suggested that she submit to a mental health
assessment.

[
48
]

Staff at the next
shelter soon shared the same concerns for the mother’s mental health.  They
contacted the Society with reports that the mother appeared to be fabricating
various narratives, was taking the child out overnight and was misrepresenting
simple facts.  For example, when R.S.A. was still an infant, staff informed the
Family Service Worker that the mother claimed to have come directly from Saudi
Arabia, but R.S.A.’s Passport indicated that she had been born in Kingston,
Ontario.  The mother was unable to provide an accurate age for R.S.A.  The
mother had several identifying documents in her possession with different
names, including one that said she was a cardiologist.

[
49
]

On September 25,
2015 shelter staff became increasingly concerned with the mother’s false
representations that she was away taking medical training.  There were strong
indications that she was involved in prostitution.  This is vigorously denied
by the mother.  Her counsel’s Factum suggests that she was away in the evenings
for religious observances.  Ultimately, mother and child were found in
Haliburton in circumstances that had been wholly misrepresented by the mother
to shelter staff.

[
50
]

As the child
appeared to be well, the mother was allowed to take her back to the shelter
with plans for York C.A.S. to investigate further.  Within a short period, the
mother resumed a pattern of being constantly out in the community, including
late at night.  Staff were suspicious that she was involved in human
trafficking.  This is vigorously denied by the mother.

[
51
]

The staff also
reported that the mother claimed that she was from Saudi Arabia, but her
documents indicated that she was born in Edmonton, Alberta
[18]
.  Her accent was inconsistent.  The staff
members soon noted an array of more false information, much of it concerning
enough to investigate.  As the staff learned more, the mother appeared to be
readying to leave the shelter.  Before the mother could permanently depart, the
Society apprehended the child.

[
52
]

In her June 2016 Affidavit
the mother states that she has no mental health issues and that she is prepared
to take a mental health assessment.  She never has.  Rather, her counsel
proposes that it is the Society’s responsibility to address and support the
mother’s mental health – and that they have not done enough.

[
53
]

In her June 13,
2016 Affidavit, the mother confirms that she was not truthful with the various
Societies, but justifies her falsehoods as being borne out of necessity – she
does not trust the Society.  She fears that her personal information will be
used against her.  Her counsel argues that R.S.A.’s well-being was never in
question and that the mother’s many misrepresentations regarding her
whereabouts, education, occupation and personal circumstances were and continue
to be irrelevant.

[
54
]

But that is simply
not the case.  At the time of apprehension R.S.A. was almost 10 months old and
had never stayed anywhere but in shelters and hotel rooms.  R.S.A. was
developmentally behind.  She was subsequently diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder
and global developmental delay.  Her significant needs were not being met by
the mother at the time of apprehension.  The mother was not even aware of the
child’s special needs until well after the apprehension.

[
55
]

Justice A. Pazaratz
stated at paragraph 43 of
Children’s Aid Society of the Niagara Region v.
S.C.
,
2008 CanLII 52309 (ON SC)
, [2008] O.J. No. 3969 (Sup. Ct.):
“no genuine issue for trial exists where there is no realistic possibility of
an outcome other than that as sought by the applicant.”

[
56
]

I find that there
is no genuine issue requiring a trial with respect to a statutory finding
pursuant to
sections 37(2)
(b) (i) and (ii) and 37(2) (g) of the
Act
.

Is there a Genuine Issue Requiring a
Trial for a Disposition for the Child Other Than Crown Wardship
?

[
57
]

Following apprehension, the Society made
extensive efforts to work with the mother, with a strong focus on mental health
supports.  Those efforts were rebuffed by the mother.

[
58
]

The mother’s access was sporadic.  When she did
attend she would often arrive late and leave early.  The mother did not
maintain ongoing contact with her worker.

[
59
]

As of November, 2016, she regularly began to
miss visits. She asked to have access visits at her home.  This was agreed by
the Society, with a pre-condition of the worker viewing the home.  Not until
December 21, 2016 was this arranged by the mother.  The home proved
satisfactory, but in the process, the Society discovered that the mother was
again pregnant.  Upon this discovery, the mother discontinued her cooperation.

[
60
]

On January 17, 2017, the worker received a
message from the mother.  The mother advised that she was overseas and that her
visits should be cancelled until January 25, 2017.  On January 22, she left
another message indicating that she was in British Columbia.  But when she
returned to Ontario, she denied that she had been overseas due to problems with
her Passport.

[
61
]

The mother’s January 31, 2017 visit was the last
time that she saw the child.  Thereafter she disappeared.  In the following
months the Society made efforts to locate the mother, particularly given
concerns as to what was happening with her pregnancy.  The Society amended its
Application to seek crown wardship.

[
62
]

On May 9, 2017 the mother somewhat surprised the
Society by attending the scheduled court date.  She reported that she was
living in Dubai, where she had given birth.  She had not brought the baby with
her.  She indicated that she was married.  She talked about plans to spend time
in Dubai caring for her new baby while travelling regularly to Canada to visit
R.S.A.  Her long term plan was for R.S.A. to live with her new family in Dubai.

[
63
]

But once again, she disappeared.  Society emails
and voicemails were unanswered until an email of November 22, 2017.  I have
reviewed that email.  The mother blames the Society for not providing email
updates to her, and she asks them to call her on a phone number as needed.  The
phone number that she provided is that of the Society.

[
64
]

A Twitter account message dated July 26, 2017
raises a question of whether the mother was in Dubai in late July.  The
mother’s Passport has not been tendered to support the mother’s claims of travelling
between Canada and Dubai.

[
65
]

No kin options have been presented.

[
66
]

R.S.A. has been in the care of the Society for
over two years.  Since being placed in care she has made some gains.  Over the
years she will need substantial support.

[
67
]

In determining whether a genuine issue exists,
the court must consider the strict time lines governing child protection
procedure. A child’s need for permanency planning is paramount.

[
68
]

It is not in a child’s best interests to delay
permanency planning.  Neither is it permitted in statute.  There is a one-year
statutory time limit for children under six years old set out in
clause 70(1)

(a) of the
Act
.  There must be an arguable notion discernible from the parent’s
evidence that they face some better prospects than what existed at the time of
the Society’s removal of the child from their care.
[19]

[
69
]

The Affidavit of the law clerk, as to her
information and belief, is wholly insufficient to such a task.  In submissions,
the mother’s counsel confirmed that her only witness at trial would be her own
law clerk.  The mother has chosen to give no direct evidence, or to provide
particulars of her evidence sufficient to satisfy tests of reliability.  A
party resisting a motion for Summary Judgment must put her best foot forward.

[
70
]

I find that there is no genuine issue requiring
a trial for a disposition for the child other than crown wardship.

Is there a Genuine Issue Requiring a
Trial as to Whether the Mother Should Have Access?

[
71
]

Section 59(2.1)
of the
Act
establishes a
presumption against access if the child is made a crown ward.  The person
seeking access has the burden of proving, on a balance of probabilities, that
the relationship between the person and the child is beneficial and meaningful
to the child; and that the ordered access will not impair the child’s future
opportunities for adoption.

[
72
]

The court is prohibited from making an access Order
with respect to a crown ward, unless the evidence demonstrates that the
relationship between the person and the child is beneficial and meaningful and
the ordered access will not impair the child’s future opportunities for
adoption.

[
73
]

Counsel for the mother makes no submissions with
respect to access.

[
74
]

In the absence of any submissions, I find that there
is no genuine issue requiring a trial as to whether the mother should have
access, or whether access would impair the child’s future opportunities to be
adopted.

______________________________

Justice
H. McGee

Released:
February 26, 2018

[1]

Children’s Aid Society of Toronto v. T. (K.)

2000 CanLII
20578

[2]
The clerk deposes that the mother has been known by three other
names than that set out in the style of cause to this Application.

[3]
The quality of the document is so very poor that no certainty can
be attached to its origin or authenticity.

[4]

Berger v. Berger
,
2016 ONCA 884
, 85 R.F.L. (7th) 259,
at para.
76
.

[5]

Berger v. Berger
,
supra
at para.
75
.

[6]

Sweda Farms Ltd. v. Egg Farmers of Ontario
,
2014 ONSC 1200

[7]
Lawyers must also guard against becoming witnesses in a proceeding:
see Rule 5.2 of the Law Society of Upper Canada’s Rules of Professional Conduct.
If the evidence of counsel or her staff person becomes necessary for trial on a
contentious issue, it may be necessary for the client to retain another law
firm as the lawyer or clerk must give evidence and be cross-examined in the
proceeding.

[8]

Victoria Mendes et al. v. Blaisdale Montessori School
,
2014
ONSC 3178
at para.
3
, aff'd
2014 ONCA 821

[9]

Mazinani v. Bindoo
,
2013 ONSC 4744
, at para.
60
.

Essa
(Township) v. Guergis

(1993),
1993 CanLII 8756 (ON CTGDDC)
, 15 O.R. (3d) 573 (Div. Crt.);
Bluestone v.
Silverman
,
2005 CanLII 27143
, at para.
8
(d).

[10]

2014 ONSC 7119

[11]

2016 ONSC 2757

[12]

R. v. Shayesteh

(1996),
1996 CanLII 882 (ON CA)
, 94 O.A.C. 81 (C.A.);
First
Capital Realty Inc. v. Centrecorp Management Services Ltd
.
(2009), 258 O.A.C.
76 (Div. Crt.)
.

[13]

Icecorp Logistics Inc. v. Goodwin
,
2011 ONSC 2924
, at para.

24
.

[14]

Jacobson v. Atlas Copco Canada Inc
.,
2015 ONSC 4
,

at paras.
31-35
;
Isakhani v. Al-Saggaf
,
2007 ONCA 539
, 40 R.F.L. (6th)
284, at para.
38
.

[15]
If the pages from the Passport are genuine, why not notarize
legible copies?

[16]
This accords with Rule 20.02 of the
Rules of Civil Procedure

which also permits Affidavits based on information and belief in the context of
